points.text: BJP remained largest party but needed coalition partners. No single party ruled alone. Power-sharing negotiations. Government formed by coalition.

points.label: Peaceful transfer
points.text: Results declared. Opposition accepted. No violence. Courts handled election disputes. Democracy survived.

slides.inSimpleWords: India's elections are massive—nearly 1 billion voters, spread over weeks, many candidates and parties competing fairly. The result: power is shared, no single group dominates.

slides.title: Challenge: Is Your School Democratic?
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma assigns: 'Look at how decisions are made in school. Which are democratic? Which aren't?'

points.label: Democratic decisions
points.text: Student council elections (free, equal voting). Class captain chosen by class vote. Debate club leadership elected by members.

points.label: Non-democratic
points.text: Principal decides curriculum (not voted). Teachers assign seats (top-down). Uniform color picked by administration (no student vote).

points.label: Mixed
points.text: School council has students + teachers + principal. Students have voice but not majority power.

example.problem: Your school wants to decide the new lunch menu. Should it be (A) Principal decides alone, or (B) All students vote?
example.solution: Vote is more democratic. But in practice, students might vote only on options the school offers (limited choice). Ideal: students suggest options, then vote.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real democracy means letting people affected by decisions have a say. Not all school decisions are democratic—some need expert choice.

slides.title: Challenge: Design a Fair Election System
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma asks: 'If you were election commissioner, how would you make India's elections fairer for rich and poor candidates equally?'

points.label: The Problem
points.text: Rich candidates win more often because they can afford TV ads and rallies. Poor candidates lose even if they're honest and capable.

points.label: Possible Solutions
points.text: (1) Limit campaign spending. (2) Give free TV time to all candidates. (3) Use grassroots media (local newspapers). (4) Fund poor candidates. (5) Require debates where poor candidates get platform.

points.label: Trade-offs
points.text: More regulations = less freedom. Spending limits can silence candidates. Free TV time is expensive. But without rules, rich dominate. Democracy needs balance.

slides.inSimpleWords: Democracy works best when poor candidates can compete fairly with rich ones. But balancing fairness and freedom is hard.

slides.title: Challenge: Democracy or Mob Rule?
slides.storyContext: Rohan poses a tough question: 'If 99% of the school voted to ban left-handed students, would that be democratic? Or tyranny?'

points.label: The Problem
points.text: Pure majority rule (51% can oppress 49%) isn't actually democracy—it's mob tyranny. Real democracy protects minorities.

points.label: Constitutional Limits
points.text: India's Constitution says even Parliament can't violate fundamental rights. Even if 100% voted to ban a religion, Supreme Court would strike it down.

points.label: The Balance
points.text: Democracy = majority rule + minority protection. Voting matters, but rights are sacred. This is the core tension in democratic theory.

points.label: Real Examples
points.text: USA South: Democracy let majorities vote for segregation. But Supreme Court and civil rights movement said NO. Courts had to force democracy to honor its own principles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Just because 51% voted for something doesn't make it democratic if it violates the rights of the 49%. Real democracy protects minorities.

slides.title: Types of Democracy Around the World
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma explains: 'Not all democracies work the same way. India has a parliamentary system. Others have presidential systems.'

points.label: Parliamentary (India, UK, Germany)
points.text: Legislature elects the executive (PM). PM answers to Parliament. If Parliament votes no-confidence, PM is out.

points.label: Presidential (USA, Brazil, Mexico)
points.text: President elected directly and rules independently from Legislature. Congress can't remove president except through impeachment.

points.label: Semi-Presidential (France, Russia)
points.text: Both President and PM. President is head of state (symbolic). PM handles daily government. Confusing, often conflicts.

points.label: Key Difference
points.text: Parliamentary: Legislature supreme. Presidential: Executive (President) more powerful. Different systems, different trade-offs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Democracies vary: some give power mainly to Parliament (India), others to an elected President (USA). Different systems, different strengths and weaknesses.

slides.title: Challenge: Strengthening Indian Democracy
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma poses: 'What could India do to make democracy work better? Reduce corruption? Fix money in politics? Improve voter awareness?'

points.label: Voter Education
points.text: More civic education in schools. Help voters understand issues, not just vote for famous people or buy elections.

points.label: Campaign Finance Reform
points.text: Limit spending. Require transparency. Level the playing field so poor candidates can compete.

points.label: Anti-Corruption Measures
points.text: Stronger oversight of elected officials. Fast-track courts for corruption cases. Publish politician's assets.

points.label: Inclusive Representation
points.text: Reservations for backward classes, SC/ST. More women in Parliament. Different communities should have voice.

slides.inSimpleWords: Democracy works best when voters are informed, money doesn't dominate, politicians aren't corrupt, and all communities have representation.

slides.title: Local Democracy: Village Panchayats
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma shares: 'Democracy doesn't just happen at national level. India's villages have their own elected councils.'

points.label: What is a Panchayat?
points.text: Elected council of 5-11 people in a village. They decide on roads, schools, water, disputes. Closer to people than Parliament.

points.label: Why It Matters
points.text: Local government is where people experience democracy directly. If panchayats are corrupt or unfair, people lose faith in democracy.

points.label: Reservation for Women
points.text: India requires at least 1/3 of panchayat seats for women. This increased women's participation and voice.

points.label: The Challenge
points.text: Upper-caste men often dominate even with women's seats. Social norms restrict women's voice. Real democracy requires cultural change, not just laws.

slides.inSimpleWords: Villages have their own elected councils (panchayats). They handle local issues. Democracy works best when it's close to people's lives.

slides.title: How a Bill Becomes Law in India
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma walks through: 'Say someone proposes a law to ban child labor. Here's how it moves through Parliament.'

points.label: Bill Introduction
points.text: An MP (government or opposition) introduces a bill in Lok Sabha (lower house). Public reading. Debate.

points.label: Committee Review
points.text: Bill sent to committee of MPs. They study it, propose amendments. Public feedback. Report back to Lok Sabha.

points.label: Vote in Lok Sabha
points.text: Full debate. All MPs vote. Needs simple majority. If passes, goes to Rajya Sabha (upper house).

points.label: Rajya Sabha & Presidential Assent
points.text: Same process in Rajya Sabha. If both pass, goes to President. President signs it. Bill becomes law.

slides.inSimpleWords: Laws go through multiple stages: committee review, floor debate, votes in both houses, presidential approval. Slow, but thorough.

slides.title: The Right to Information: Democracy's Accountability Tool
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma explains: 'In India, citizens have a right to ask the government for information. This is called RTI (Right to Information).'

points.label: What is RTI?
points.text: Law (2005) gives any citizen the right to request government documents and data. Govt must respond within 30 days.

points.label: Example
points.text: A journalist files RTI asking: 'How much money did the city spent on contracts to Company X?' City can't refuse. Must disclose (unless it's classified).

points.label: Impact
points.text: RTI exposed corruption, illegal deals, wasteful spending. Journalists, activists, and ordinary people use it to hold government accountable.

points.label: Why It Matters
points.text: Transparency is democracy's oxygen. If citizens can access info, they can catch corruption. If secret, abuse grows.

slides.inSimpleWords: India's Right to Information law lets citizens demand answers from government. Transparency keeps democracy honest.

slides.title: Judicial Review: Courts as Democracy's Guardian
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma explains: 'India's Supreme Court has power to strike down laws—even laws passed by Parliament. This is checks and balances.'

points.label: What is Judicial Review
points.text: Courts can declare laws or actions unconstitutional and void them. A law passed by 100% of Parliament is invalid if it violates the Constitution.

points.label: Example
points.text: Dowry prohibition (1961): Outlawed bride-price. Constitutional. Court upheld it. Sati prohibition (1829): Outlawed widow-burning. Constitutional. Court upheld it.

points.label: Who Can Challenge
points.text: Any citizen can challenge any law in court. File a 'public interest petition.' Supreme Court listens. Rich or poor, your case matters.

points.label: Why It Works
points.text: Democratic majorities can oppress minorities. Judicial review protects minorities. Courts say: 'Constitution is supreme. Laws must respect it.'

slides.inSimpleWords: Courts can veto laws that violate the Constitution. This stops majorities from oppressing minorities and keeps democracy honest.

slides.title: Challenge: Evaluating Democratic Health
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma asks: 'How do we know if a country is truly democratic? What are the signs?'

points.label: Free & Fair Elections
points.text: Multiple parties compete. Voters can choose. Losers accept results peacefully. No rigging.

points.label: Free Press
points.text: Journalists can criticize government. Media is independent. No censorship.

points.label: Independent Courts
points.text: Courts rule against government if law is unjust. Not puppets of executive.

points.label: Actual Participation
points.text: Citizens feel empowered. Panchayats work. Civil society is active. Not just elections, but real involvement.

points.label: Peaceful Alternation
points.text: Ruling party loses, accepts it. No violence. New party takes office. This has happened in India 8 times.

slides.inSimpleWords: A healthy democracy has free elections, independent courts, free press, peaceful power transfers, and active citizens—not just voting.

slides.title: Election Commission: Umpire of Democracy
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma explains: 'India's Election Commission is an independent body that runs elections. No government interference.'

points.label: What They Do
points.text: Conduct elections. Check voter rolls. Ensure secret ballot. Prevent fraud. Monitor campaign spending. Hear complaints. Announce results.

points.label: Independence
points.text: EC reports to President, not PM. Can't be fired by government. Has power to freeze assets if candidate spends illegally.

points.label: Challenges
points.text: Money still influences elections. Not all EC orders are followed. Some politicians ignore spending limits. But EC's independence is real and strong.

points.label: Why It Matters
points.text: If government ran elections, it would rig them for itself. EC as neutral umpire (imperfect, but trying) keeps elections fair.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Election Commission is democracy's umpire: independent, monitors elections, prevents fraud. Imperfect, but crucial.

slides.title: Democratic Culture: Beyond Laws
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma concludes: 'Democracy is more than laws and institutions. It's a culture—a way of thinking and acting.'

points.label: Respecting Opponents
points.text: In true democracy, you argue with your opponent but accept they have a right to argue back. You lose elections without violence.

points.label: Listening to Dissent
points.text: If government listens to critics, democracy works. If government silences critics (arrests, censors), democracy dies—even if elections happen.

points.label: Civic Duty
points.text: Democracy needs citizens to vote, serve on juries, follow laws, pay taxes. If citizens are apathetic, democracy weakens.

points.label: The Real Challenge
points.text: Making democracy work isn't just about Constitution or courts. It's about people choosing to respect each other, follow rules, and participate.

slides.inSimpleWords: Democracy survives when people respect opponents, listen to dissent, and participate. Laws matter, but culture matters more.

slides.title: What You Learned: Democracy Fundamentals
slides.storyContext: As Rohan leaves class, he feels proud. 'My vote mattered today. In many countries, I'd have no say in who leads. I'm lucky.'

points.text: Democracy = rule by the people through voting and representation. Power rests with citizens, not a king or dictator.
Key features: free elections, equal votes, secret ballot, rule of law, freedom of speech, peaceful transfer of power, accountability.
Merits: peaceful conflict resolution, prevents abuse of power, respects equality, encourages participation, ensures accountability.
Challenges: uninformed voters, false promises, money in politics, majority tyranny, slow decisions, unequal influence.
India is a representative democracy. Citizens vote for leaders every 5 years. Parliament makes laws. Courts protect rights.
Separation of powers: Executive, Legislative, Judicial branches check each other so no one person grabs all power.
Constitution protects fundamental rights. Courts can strike down laws that violate the Constitution.
Democracy is not perfect but better than dictatorship because power can change hands peacefully and ordinary people have a say.

slides.inSimpleWords: Democracy lets people rule themselves through voting. It's slower than dictatorship but fairer, more peaceful, and protects everyone's rights.
